Every spring I read about four hundred artist statements for one open call, and I can tell you exactly what happens in the first thirty seconds. I look for a sentence in which the artist does something. Not the practice, not the work, not the investigation. The artist. I record, I collect, I interview. If I reach the end of the first paragraph and I still cannot say what this person physically does in the studio, I move on. I am not proud of it, but that is the reality of a jury with four hundred files. The second thing I look for is one idea I have not already read that morning. Everybody interrogates something. Everybody foregrounds something. Those words have been used so often that they have stopped carrying anything. The statements that stay with me are usually the plainest ones, written by people who clearly know the theory and decided not to show off with it.

Most of the artists who come to me have already written the statement, and it is almost always too abstract, not too simple. So the first thing we do together is find the nouns that are hiding verbs. Documentation, representation, investigation. For each one I ask a very plain question: who does it, and to what? The answer usually goes straight into the new version, as a sentence with the artist as the subject. Then we keep the two or three abstract nouns that are genuinely doing work, the ones with no shorter way to say them. Materiality is often one of those. Finally, I ask the artist to read the whole thing aloud to somebody outside the art world. If that person can repeat back what is at stake in one sentence, the statement is finished. If they cannot, we distill it again. It usually takes three rounds, and it is always the third version that gets sent.
